title: The Effects of Oral Contraceptives on Exercise Performance in Women: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
authors: Elliott-Sale KJ, McNulty KL, Ansdell P, Goodall S, Hicks KM, Thomas K, Swinton PA, Dolan E
population: Women using oral contraceptives compared with naturally menstruating women or with OCP withdrawal; 42 studies, 590 participants
findings: 42 studies and 590 participants included; 83% of studies were graded moderate, low or very low quality and 17% high quality.

Between-group: probability of a small effect (d >= 0.2) favouring OCP users was effectively zero (p < 0.001); probability favouring naturally menstruating women was 0.40 (OCP withdrawal vs early follicular) and 0.19 (OCP consumption vs non-early-follicular phases).
Within-group: almost zero probability of a small effect in either direction when comparing OCP consumption with withdrawal (p <= 0.001); performance was consistent across the OCP cycle.

Authors conclude OCP use might result in slightly inferior performance on average but any group-level effect is most likely trivial; current evidence does not warrant general guidance and an individualised approach is suggested.
limitations: Mostly low-quality studies, large between-study variance, oral contraceptives only (not other hormonal methods).
implications: Apply no performance or load adjustment for oral contraceptive use; treat contraceptive status as an optional annotation.
Pair with HRV findings: contraceptive users have lower HRV baselines, so use individual baselines, not population norms.

verification.notes: Added by verifier. Crossref (Sports Med, 2020-07, first author Elliott-Sale) matches; Europe PMC abstract (PMID 32666247) supports all numbers.
